items.headline: U.S. Textbook Authors Sue OpenAI for Copyright Infringement
items.excerpt: The Textbook & Academic Authors Association-linked plaintiffs allege OpenAI ingested their textbooks without licence. Authors warn that if LLMs keep absorbing new editions, instructors may drop textbook adoptions for AI 'substitutes'.

items.headline: Harriman House claims trade publishing first with 'AI-facilitated' Raoul Pal book
items.excerpt: Harriman House says it has produced a trade title with an AI-facilitated workflow built around Raoul Pal's existing body of work, describing it as a first for trade publishing.

items.headline: Study Finds 63% of Religion Books on Amazon Likely AI Written
items.excerpt: A survey by AI detector Originality.ai of 2,034 paperback religion books on Amazon found the majority were likely AI-written, including roughly three-quarters of titles on Hinduism, Taoism and witchcraft. AI titles were shorter and cheaper than human-authored ones.

items.headline: Guest Post — AI Can Find the Article. Can It Tell Which Version It Used?
items.excerpt: AI research assistants surface scholarly content but routinely blur which version of record they drew on. The authors argue persistent identifiers are now core publishing infrastructure, not metadata housekeeping.

items.headline: Book Marketing, AI Book Discoverability, And Resilience, With Ricardo Fayet
items.excerpt: Reedsy co-founder Ricardo Fayet on how books now reach readers through AI recommendation surfaces rather than search, and what indie authors should change about metadata, positioning and marketing as a result.

items.headline: Amazon is buying and scanning books to train AI
items.excerpt: Amazon is buying used and remaindered print books in bulk, scanning them for AI training data, and destroying the originals — a practice Friedman notes leans on outdated inventory rather than high-value titles.

items.headline: AI companies are buying hardcover books and destroying them
items.excerpt: Anthropic and Amazon are bulk-buying pre-2022 print books to harvest clean, human-written text free of synthetic 'AI slop' — bookshops in the US, UK, Europe and Australia report unusual bulk orders.

items.headline: Now Amazon is destroying rare books to train its AI
items.excerpt: Lit Hub's take on the 404 Media report that Amazon is buying massive quantities of books, scanning them for AI training data and destroying them in the process — with rare titles potentially lost for good.

items.headline: Self-Publishing News: Anthropic Adds Watermarks
items.excerpt: ALLi's weekly indie-author news round-up on Anthropic adding watermarks to Claude output, and what invisible AI provenance markers mean for authors who use assistive AI in drafting and editing.

items.headline: Self-Publishing News: Destroying Books to Train AI
items.excerpt: ALLi's news round-up for indie authors on the destructive book-scanning pipelines feeding AI training sets, and the rights and consent questions it raises for self-published print titles.

items.headline: Podcast: Amazon Rips Up Rare Books
items.excerpt: ALLi's podcast unpacks Amazon's rare-book destruction for AI training and what indie authors can do about how their own catalogues are ingested.

items.headline: Around the Book World: August 17, 2026
items.excerpt: Editor-in-chief Andrew Richard Albanese's weekly review of international publishing headlines, including AI training, licensing and rights-transparency developments.
